t.E123.agn: In its 2010 re-evaluation EFSA concluded that amaranth is not genotoxic or carcinogenic, but lowered the acceptable daily intake (ADI) to 0.15 mg/kg body weight (the SCF value from 1984 was 0.8 mg/kg). It reported that estimated exposure in children was about 30 times below this limit, while in adults regularly consuming very high amounts of Americano the limit could be exceeded by up to 6 times.
t.E123.body: In rats, only about 3% of orally ingested amaranth is absorbed. The dye is split at the azo bond by gut bacteria; what is found in urine and bile is mainly the products of this breakdown (aminonaphthalene sulphonic acids).
t.E123.eff.0.t: The daily limit may be exceeded
t.E123.eff.0.w: Adults regularly consuming very high amounts of Americano
t.E123.eval: Banned in the US in 1976 (as Red No. 2); in the EU it is authorised only in a limited range of products.
t.E123.prod: An azo dye produced by chemical synthesis.
t.E123.regx.0: Re-evaluated; ADI lowered to 0.15 mg/kg body weight. In the EU authorised only in aperitif drinks and fish roe.
t.E123.summary: A synthetic, dark red azo dye. In the EU it is authorised in a very limited range of products (some aperitif wines, fish roe).
t.E123.what: A synthetic azo colour that gives food a red colour.
t.agency.FDA_banned_1976: Banned for use in food in the US.
